problem_markdown: Set $P_1(x)=x^2-2$ and $P_{j+1}(x)=P_j(x)^2-2$. Prove that $P_n(x)-x$ has only real, simple roots for every positive integer $n$.
solutions_markdown: Let $N=2^n$. Induction using $2\cos(2t)=(2\cos t)^2-2$ gives $P_n(2\cos t)=2\cos Nt$. Thus roots arise from $t=2k\pi/(N-1)$ and $t=2k\pi/(N+1)$ in $[0,\pi]$. The first family has $N/2$ members and the second $N/2+1$. Their only common member is zero: since $\gcd(N-1,N+1)=1$, equality of the fractions forces both numerators to be zero within the specified range. Cosine is injective on $[0,\pi]$, giving exactly $N$ distinct real roots. The polynomial has degree $N$, so these are all its roots and each is simple.
